value: wild western fence lizards fled at longer distances from an approaching person wearing a red T-shirt than a dark blue one (p = 0.033, Cohen's d = 0.83)
units: categorical (flight initiation distance by observer T-shirt colour; F test, post hoc p corrected for multiple comparisons)

source.authors: Breanna J. Putman, Jonathan P. Drury, Daniel T. Blumstein, Gregory B. Pauly
source.title: Fear no colors? Observer clothing color influences lizard escape behavior

method: behavioural: field flight-initiation-distance trials, one person approaching wild lizards in a T-shirt of one of four colours (dark blue, light blue, grey, red)
conditions: Wild lizards at two Southern California sites, Griffith Park (heavily used public park) and Stunt Ranch (restricted reserve). 114 trials in all: 15 dark blue, 14 light blue, 15 grey, 15 red at Griffith Park and 14, 14, 13, 14 at Stunt Ranch; the Results do not give the number of individual lizards, and repeat trials on one individual were avoided by walking in one direction and not sampling a location twice. Shirts were worn in random order and the colour changed every 3 to 4 trials per day. Dark and light blue were chosen to resemble the males' blue throat and abdominal patches; colour and luminance contrasts against the background were computed with a receptor-noise model using the collared lizard's cone sensitivities as a proxy because Sceloporus values are unavailable, and luminance contrast was highest for light blue, then grey, red, dark blue. Overall, T-shirt colour affected FID (F = 2.89, p = 0.039). The model included start distance and distance to refuge as covariates: start distance explained significant variation in FID (F = 5.23, p = 0.024), distance to refuge did not (F = 1.83, p = 0.179). Sex had no effect on FID (t89 = 0.345, p = 0.731) and was dropped from later analyses; the sex composition of the sample is not given. One person performed all trials, approaching at a standardised 0.5 m/s, on warm sunny days (> 22 C) between 0900 and 1300 h; only relatively large adults were sampled. Nulls: red v light blue FID was only near-significant (p = 0.082, d = 0.68); site (human activity) had no effect on FID (F = 1.51, p = 0.222); the colour x site interaction was not significant (p = 0.927). Capture probability also varied with colour (chi2 = 8.32, p = 0.040; 84 % with dark blue, nearly half that with grey or red). The shirts differ in more than hue, and one approaching person is the stimulus; a fear response to a coloured shirt, not a threshold, acuity or colour-discrimination measure.
quote: After correcting for multiple comparisons, we found that lizards fled at longer distances when approached with red compared to dark blue (Fig 1), a difference with a large effect (p = 0.033, Cohen’s d = 0.83).
note: Sentence read in pieces joined at 'distances' | 'when approached' and 'dark blue' | 'a difference'; the printed '(Fig 1),' was confirmed in a second pass. Crossref single-DOI lookup: four authors in the order printed, PLOS ONE 12(8) e0182146, issued 2017-08-09, CC BY 4.0 vor; page prints CC BY 4.0. Family and order from the Reptile Database page for Sceloporus occidentalis BAIRD & GIRARD, 1852 (Higher Taxa: Phrynosomatidae, Sceloporinae, Iguania, Sauria, Squamata); the family is not in the paper. Not on main or any desk branch (grep of 0182146 and Sceloporus occidentalis). Curly apostrophe in 'Cohen’s' as printed (audit 356).

value: in a Y-maze with a food cue in one arm, 12 % of snails in acidified seawater (pH 7.6) chose the food side against 67 % in control seawater (pH 8.1) in the 2021 10-min set
units: categorical (% of snails choosing the food-cue arm, Fisher's exact test)

source.authors: Maria Manz, Joshua Lord, Melissa Morales
source.title: Ocean Acidification Impedes Foraging Behavior in the Mud Snail Ilyanassa obsoleta
source.journal: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering 11(3): 623

method: behavioural: Y-maze choice test, water from a header tank carrying the food cue entering one fork and seawater of the same pH only entering the other; time-limited trials
conditions: Snails collected from the intertidal zone of Raritan Bay, Cliffwood Beach, New Jersey and used within two months of collection, held at about pH 8.1, 25 C, 25 ppt. Control seawater pH 8.1; acidified pH 7.6 made by bubbling 1200 ppm CO2 air into a 12 L tank. The sentence is the first 2021 set (33 control and 33 acidified snails, 10 min limit, Hikari sinking carnivore pellets of fish and krill as the cue; Figure 2 caption sample sizes). Fisher's exact test for this set p < 0.001 (the Results sentence after the quote); Table A1 counts for the set: acidified 4 food, 11 empty, 18 no decision; control 22 food, 4 empty, 7 no decision. Other sets: 2017 (20 and 20 snails, 20 min, crushed mussel Geukensia demissa) acidified snails were less successful but the difference was non-significant (Fisher p > 0.05); second 2021 set (16 control, 26 acidified, 5 min) food choice 50 v 16 %, empty-arm choice 0 v 42 %, p = 0.002; no-decision snails were recorded (21 % control, 55 % acidified in the 10 min set). The Methods do not say whether the food arm was randomised or alternated, whether snails were starved, whether each snail was tested once, or give sex or size; sets differed in maze shape, time limit, food and researcher. Percentages quoted for pooled results differ between Results and Discussion (control 84 v 87 or 88 %, acidified 27 v 36 %), so only the single-set sentence is used. Attraction of snails to a food odour in control water; the empty-arm share for the 10 min set is not given in the sentence, and there is no threshold or non-detection disclosure.
quote: In the second experiment (2021, 10 min time limit), snails in the acidified treatment were more than five times less likely to successfully choose the food side of the Y-maze (12%) than in the control treatments (67% success).
note: Sentence read in two abutting pieces ('more than five times' | 'less likely') with start and end seen; the Results call it 'the second experiment' while the Methods call it the first set in 2021 (the 2017 set being the first experiment overall). Crossref single-DOI lookup: three authors in the order printed, volume 11, issue 3, 623, issued 2023-03-16, CC BY 4.0 vor; MDPI page metadata CC BY 3.0. Family and order from OBIS (api.obis.org/v3/taxon/Ilyanassa obsoleta: Nassariidae, Neogastropoda, accepted); neither is printed in the paper. gbif-names.tsv lists Nassa obsoleta as a synonym of Ilyanassa obsoleta; OBIS gives Tritia obsoleta (Say, 1822) as a superseded combination with Ilyanassa obsoleta the accepted name (audit 356). Not on main or any desk branch (grep of Ilyanassa and the DOI).

value: freely flying workers chose colours of higher spectral purity and preferred bluish colours
units: categorical (dual-choice preference for spectral purity and dominant wavelength; Wilcoxon tests)

source.authors: Sebastian Koethe, Sarah Banysch, Isabel Alves-dos-Santos, Klaus Lunau
source.title: Spectral purity, intensity and dominant wavelength: Disparate colour preferences of two Brazilian stingless bee species

method: behavioural: dual-choice tests between pigment colour stimuli differing in dominant wavelength, spectral purity or intensity, 57 choices per bee
conditions: Two stingless bee nests on the Universidade de Sao Paulo campus (the Melipona bicolor nest inside a laboratory with an outside entrance, the Partamona helleri nest outdoors); the paper does not say whether the colonies were wild or managed. 24 P. helleri and 20 M. bicolor flower-experienced, freely flying workers, individually marked with nail polish; M. bicolor workers were trained individually, P. helleri workers were caught at a feeder. Stimuli were artist pigments mixed with black, white or grey pressed into culture dishes (six colour categories of four stimuli each), reflectance measured with a spectrometer at 45 degrees and placed in Chittka's colour hexagon using Melipona quadrifasciata photoreceptor sensitivities as a proxy, D65 light and a grey background; spectral purity is hexagon distance and intensity the mean receptor excitation. Panel tilted 45 degrees, two stimuli 5 cm from the midpoint, sucrose offered on a landing platform beneath each stimulus; bees were first trained to both sides with empty lids so position was not rewarded. Each bee made 57 dual choices in semi-randomised order, one decision per foraging bout, stimuli cleaned after use, presentation order reversed for some bees. P. helleri statistics (Results): spectral purity W = 98, p = 0.0003 (Wilcoxon), intensity no effect (W = 93, p = 0.236); the Results text gives no test statistic for dominant wavelength (Figures 2 and 3 compare pooled choices by GLMM with Tukey all-pair comparisons). P. helleri: blue and UV-absorbing white were chosen most (108 of 144 tests) and red least (17 of 144) according to the tool-read Results summary. Same paper: Melipona bicolor showed no preference for spectral purity (t = -0.6589, df = 9, p = 0.5264), intensity (t = -0.8655, df = 11, p = 0.4053) or dominant wavelength; the degrees of freedom are below the 20 bees tested and the paper's Results do not say why. Preference for stimuli all rewarded with sucrose, not a detection or discrimination threshold.
quote: The results show that P. helleri chose colours of higher spectral purity and preferred bluish colours, while M. bicolor made generalized colour choices.
note: Sentence read in two abutting pieces (comma join), start and end seen. The Results sentence with W = 98 and W = 93 was read only in fragments and is not the quote. Crossref single-DOI lookup: four authors in the order printed, PLOS ONE 13(9) e0204663, issued 2018-09-28, CC BY 4.0 vor; page prints a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Family and order Apidae, Hymenoptera as on main for Partamona helleri (canon-3 rows); the paper names only the tribe Meliponini. Not on main or any desk branch (grep of 0204663).

value: colour preferences seem to be absent in dual-choice tests of dominant wavelength, spectral purity and intensity
units: categorical (dual-choice preference for spectral purity, intensity and dominant wavelength; Student's t-tests)

source.authors: Sebastian Koethe, Sarah Banysch, Isabel Alves-dos-Santos, Klaus Lunau
source.title: Spectral purity, intensity and dominant wavelength: Disparate colour preferences of two Brazilian stingless bee species

method: behavioural: dual-choice tests between pigment colour stimuli differing in dominant wavelength, spectral purity or intensity, 57 choices per bee
conditions: Two stingless bee nests on the Universidade de Sao Paulo campus (the Melipona bicolor nest inside a laboratory with an outside entrance, the Partamona helleri nest outdoors); the paper does not say whether the colonies were wild or managed. 24 P. helleri and 20 M. bicolor flower-experienced, freely flying workers, individually marked with nail polish; M. bicolor workers were trained individually, P. helleri workers were caught at a feeder. Stimuli were artist pigments mixed with black, white or grey pressed into culture dishes (six colour categories of four stimuli each), reflectance measured with a spectrometer at 45 degrees and placed in Chittka's colour hexagon using Melipona quadrifasciata photoreceptor sensitivities as a proxy, D65 light and a grey background; spectral purity is hexagon distance and intensity the mean receptor excitation. Panel tilted 45 degrees, two stimuli 5 cm from the midpoint, sucrose offered on a landing platform beneath each stimulus; bees were first trained to both sides with empty lids so position was not rewarded. Each bee made 57 dual choices in semi-randomised order, one decision per foraging bout, stimuli cleaned after use, presentation order reversed for some bees. Results statistics: no preference for spectral purity (t = -0.6589, df = 9, p = 0.5264) or intensity (t = -0.8655, df = 11, p = 0.4053, Student's t-test); for dominant wavelength the Results say only that workers showed no distinct preferences (no statistic in the text). A null for colour preference in this species; the stimulus set was pigments with a three-receptor model borrowed from M. quadrifasciata, so the null does not show the bees cannot discriminate the colours. The degrees of freedom (9 and 11) are below the 20 bees tested and the Results do not say why. Same paper: Partamona helleri preferred spectrally purer and bluish colours (W = 98, p = 0.0003) and ignored intensity (W = 93, p = 0.236).
quote: The results of P. helleri are consistent with findings for honeybees and bumblebees, while colour preferences in M. bicolor seem to be absent.
note: Sentence read in two abutting pieces, start and end seen. The Results t statistics are quoted from a fragment read at the page, not from the quote. value: females were significantly repelled by volatiles from Coriandrum sativum (chi2 = 9, df = 1, p < 0.01) and Petroselinum crispum (chi2 = 6.76, df = 1, p = 0.01) in a Y-tube (n = 25 females)
units: categorical (Y-tube choice, chi-squared goodness of fit)

source.authors: Camila C. Santander, Marta V. Albornoz, M. Fernanda Flores, Eduardo Oyanedel, Wilson Barros-Parada, Armando Alfaro-Tapia
source.title: Plant Volatiles and Essential Oils Induce Sex-Specific Behavioral Responses and Concentration-Dependent Toxicity in the Invasive Pest Bagrada hilaris

method: behavioural: single-insect Y-tube olfactometer (glass, 130 degrees between arms, charcoal-purified air at 0.2 L/min), potted plant volatiles against potting mix alone, up to 5 min to choose
conditions: Colony founded from adults collected in two organic cabbage fields in Quillota, Chile and periodically restocked with field-collected insects (25 C, 16:8 L:D, fed cabbage leaves); newly emerged adults sexed during copulation (so tested insects had mated; age not otherwise given), starved 5 h, each insect used once. Nine aromatic and ornamental plant species were tested; valid responses were recorded from 25 males and 25 females per species (the Methods say 25 to 35 individuals of each sex were tested; insects that did not move toward either arm within 5 min were scored as non-responses and excluded, their number shown only in Figures 1 and 2, so the test is of responders). Pot and treatment sides were assigned randomly and alternated every 10 replicates, the Y-tube was rotated between replicates and cleaned every 10 replicates, runs 11:00 to 17:00. Males (n = 25) were repelled only by Pelargonium hortorum volatiles (chi2 = 6.67, df = 1, p = 0.01). Nulls: Pelargonium hortorum had no effect on females (p = 0.32), C. sativum had none on males (p = 0.84), and the remaining species had no effect on either sex; Ocimum basilicum attracted males (chi2 = 4.48, p = 0.03). Essential oils of the three plants (hexane control) repelled both sexes over concentration-dependent ranges that differed by oil, and the repellency index did not differ by sex. Repellency of plant volatiles at an unmeasured emission rate, not a detection threshold; a failure to repel (including the nulls above) does not show that the odour was not detected, and the authors call the responses generally weaker than expected.
quote: Adult females of B. hilaris (n = 25) were significantly repelled by volatiles from C. sativum (χ2 = 9; df = 1; p < 0.01) and P. crispum (χ2 = 6.76; df = 1; p = 0.01).
note: Sentence read in two abutting pieces ('p < 0.01)' | 'and P. crispum'), start and end seen; 'χ2' as printed. value: parent females spent less time on nest sanitation when ferret-urine predator cues were placed in the nest-box
units: categorical (parental behaviour by odour treatment; ANOVA)

source.authors: Irene Saavedra, Gustavo Tomás, Luisa Amo
source.title: Assessing behavioral sex differences to chemical cues of predation risk while provisioning nestlings in a hole-nesting bird

method: behavioural: field scent test, odour-soaked absorbent papers hidden in occupied nest-boxes at nestling day 8, parental behaviour filmed for 60 min and scored blind
conditions: Wild blue tits in Pyrenean oak forests (Zaragoza and Teruel provinces, Spain); 45 nests used of 250 boxes. Treatments: ferret (mustelid) urine scent as the predator cue (19 nests), rabbit scent as a non-predatory odour control (16) and water as an odourless control (10); treatments were assigned alternately to nests with similar brood size and hatching date and randomised with respect to time of day. Parents were captured with nest-box traps when nestlings were 6 days old, two days before the trial, and sexed by brood patch (present only in females); the authors say the capture may have made adults more cautious. Female sanitation differed by treatment (F2,41 = 3.81, p = 0.03), significant only between the water control and the predator cue (p = 0.04); no statistics are printed for the other two contrasts. Odour donors were two adult male ferrets and two adult male rabbits; two absorbent papers (11 x 13 cm) per box. Regardless of odour, females entered sooner (F1,42 = 208.51, p = 0.003) and provisioned more (F1,40 = 28.69, p < 0.001) than males. Nulls: treatment had no significant effect on latency to first entry, provisioning rate or number of begging nestlings, and no treatment x sex interaction was significant; the authors conclude that the response was not sex-dependent. Males never sanitised, so the sanitation result is for females only. The sanitation difference was significant only between the water control and the predator cue, and the paper reports no significant difference involving the rabbit control in the tool-read summary. A reaction to a predator-urine lure at an unmeasured dose; the unresponsive measures do not show that the odour was undetected, and there is no threshold.
quote: However, females reduced time devoted to nest sanitation activities when predator chemical cues were detected inside the nest-box, likely as an anti-predatory strategy to minimize their own risk of predation.
note: Sentence read in three abutting pieces (breaks after 'activities' and 'strategy'), start and end seen. Results figures (F2,41 = 3.81, p = 0.03; control v predator p = 0.04) come from the Results as read through the tool summary, not from the quote.
